rv.q: It feels ungrateful to dismiss any new musical that offers Donna Murphy a chance to play a Nazi-oppressed Polish star
Even in this well-intentioned but wobbly vehicle, Murphy's work demonstrates again that she's one of musical theater's most dramatically nuanced performers.
Without Ms. Murphy this well-meaning Roundabout Theater Company production — which has a book and lyrics by Iris Rainer Dart and songs by Mike Stoller and Artie Butler — would be thin treacle indeed.

Unfortunately, the book and lyrics — by "Beaches" novelist and first-time Broadway story writer Iris Rainer Dart — and music — by Mike Stoller ("Smokey Joe's Cafe") and Artie Butler (who wrote the pop standard "Here's to Life") — don't always rise to Murphy's high standard.
But other than two of these zany flashbacks and one effective, especially dramatic ballad (“Selective Memory”) from Murphy, it’s a long evening filled with threadbare melodramatic machinations.
Here, she works tirelessly to perform CPR on a DOA show.
The People in the Picture is a well-intentioned musical about the Holocaust that suffers from a fatal case of good intentions.
As The People in the Picture aptly displays, talent is sometimes all artists have left — and talent is very much on display in this taut, penetrating show.
There are groaners galore in “Picture” -- I hope it’s the only time I’ll ever hear “Jerusalem” rhymed with “bamboozle ’em” -- but I’m going to assume they’re intended.
The People in the Picture is a show that wants desperately to be important, but settles for being merely earnest.
Fortunately, the score doesn't hit us over the head like the book.

Everything ultimately comes together in a scene of great emotion, but one that's out of step both with the tone of the rest of the play and with what we've learned of Raisel as a character. "The People in the Picture" seems to have been a labor of love for Dart, but, without freshness, wit or dramatic imagination, it's not much of a musical.
The credentials may be promising, but the resulting picture isn't pretty.
It’s an unforgettable tale and a graceful production.
The People in the Picture is an ambitious and well-meaning show, to be sure.

cn.t: Critics find this Holocaust-themed musical earnest but misguided, with tonal inconsistencies and heavy-handed sentimentality undermining its good intentions. Donna Murphy's performance earns praise, but can't save the show's awkward mix of tragedy and Borscht Belt humor.

sg.ra: SeatPlan names Center Orchestra rows E-G as the best seats overall, citing 'a winning mix of perfect proximity and elevated view over the heads in front' on a good rake with a low stage. Headout notes the 'outstanding inclination' keeps sightlines clear from middle rows. AVFMS Row D seat 2: 'Perfect view with unlimited legroom.' 16-row section seats ~350 of the 413 total; low stage means front rows don't require neck strain.

SeatPlan explicitly names Left and Right Mezzanine as 'the best value seats at the Laura Pels Theatre,' citing cheap tickets vs. central Orchestra with 'a clear and close view.' Only 3 rows (AA/BB/CC), under 100 seats — feels intimate and close to stage. Headout confirms 'very little restriction from the Mezzanine overhang at the back' of the Orchestra, meaning the Mezzanine itself is close/low. Row BB flagged by Headout as a specific value row.
